result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.which_loops()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find edge IDs of self-loops (edges from a node to itself). ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L36780-L36868){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.which_loops() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Which loops](/assets/graphs/which-loops.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Four nodes in a row joined by edges 1, 2, 3, with self-loops 4 and 5 on A and 6 on C in the accent color. The card returns the self-loop edge ids 4, 5, 6." width="100%"} Returns a list of edge IDs for all edges where the source node equals the target node. Self-loops are common in certain network types like state machines, chemical reactions, or social networks (self-mentions). Because many algorithms either ignore self-loops or behave unexpectedly with them, it is often worth checking for them before analysis. This method is useful for: - detecting whether a graph has any self-loops (an empty list means none) - inspecting or editing the loop edges themselves (their IDs can be passed to edge methods such as `get_edge()`) - auditing data imports, where self-loops often signal a data-entry error The graph is not modified. Every self-loop is reported, including several on the same node, and both directed and undirected graphs are supported. For per-node counts use `count_loops()`, and to delete all self-loops use `remove_selfloops()`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of edge IDs representing self-loops, in the order the edges are stored (normally the order they were added). Empty if no self-loops exist. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Enumerates every edge whose source and target coincide in a single $O(E)$ pass. Directed and undirected graphs are both supported; a single node can carry multiple self-loops and each such edge appears in the returned list. Self-loops distort several graph statistics (they inflate degree by two rather than one, break certain adjacency-matrix identities, and confuse some spectral bounds), so removing them before analysis is a common preprocessing step: `count_loops()` gives the per-node totals, and `remove_selfloops()` clears them in a single pass. ## Examples {.doc-examples} In a directed graph, a self-loop is any edge whose source and target are the same node: ::: {#89de4318 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(directed=True) g.add_nodes(["Alice", "Bob", "Carol"]) g.add_edges( [ ("Alice", "Bob"), ("Alice", "Alice"), # Self-loop ("Bob", "Carol"), ("Carol", "Carol"), # Self-loop ] ) # Returns 2 (Alice->Alice and Carol->Carol) len(g.which_loops()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: The returned values are edge IDs, so they can be looked up to see which nodes carry the loops: ::: {#d960d286 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} [g.get_label_from_id(g.get_edge(eid).source) for eid in g.which_loops()] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ['Alice', 'Carol'] ``` ::: ::: In a state machine, self-loops naturally represent states that can transition back to themselves, like a "wait" or "retry" state: ::: {#02f38471 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} fsm = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["Idle", "Processing", "Complete"]) .add_edges( [ ("Idle", "Processing"), ("Processing", "Processing"), # Wait state ("Processing", "Complete"), ("Complete", "Idle"), ] ) ) # Returns 1 (the Processing -> Processing wait state) len(fsm.which_loops()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 1 ``` ::: :::
